parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State and explain whether a neutron is a fundamental particle.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what the word fundamental means - can the particle be split into anything smaller, or is it built from quarks?
parts.proper_answer: No, a neutron is not fundamental because it is made up of quarks (one up quark and two down quarks).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Fundamental Really Means**
Think of fundamental as having no internal structure. An electron is fundamental because as far as we know it cannot be broken down further. A proton and a neutron are different - they belong to a family called hadrons.

Step 2: **Inside a Neutron**
A neutron is a hadron made of three quarks held together by the strong force. Its quark combination is $udd$ - one up quark and two down quarks. Because it has internal structure, it is not a fundamental particle.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem: A proton in a stationary nucleus decays.
parts.text: State the two leptons that are produced by the decay.
hints: Hint 1: A proton changing to a neutron inside a nucleus is beta-plus decay. Recall which two light lepton particles must appear to conserve charge and lepton number.
Hint 2: One is the antimatter version of the electron, and the other is a near-massless neutral lepton that carries away energy.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the Decay**
A proton in a nucleus turning into a neutron can only happen by the weak interaction. This is $\beta^{+}$ decay:
$$p \rightarrow n + e^{+} + \nu_{e}$$
Charge is conserved: $+1$ on the left, $0 + (+1) + 0$ on the right.

Step 2: **Pick Out the Leptons**
Leptons are the family that are fundamental and do not feel the strong force. In this equation the proton and neutron are hadrons, so the two leptons are the positron $e^{+}$ (also called the $\beta^{+}$ particle) and the electron neutrino $\nu_{e}$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
Part of the energy released by the decay is given to the two leptons.

State two possible forms of the remainder of the released energy.
hints: Hint 1: Energy released in a nuclear decay does not all appear as one type. Think about what moving particles gain and what the excited daughter nucleus can emit.
Hint 2: Consider the kinetic energy carried by massive products and the electromagnetic radiation emitted when a nucleus de-excites or when antimatter meets matter.
parts.proper_answer: Kinetic energy of the positron (and electron) and gamma ($\gamma$) radiation.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Energy Must Go Somewhere**
The mass lost in the decay appears as energy. Some is already given as kinetic and rest energy to the two leptons. The rest must appear in other products from the decay.

Step 2: **Two Other Forms**
One form is kinetic energy of massive particles produced, such as the emitted positron (and electrons in the atom). The other common form is electromagnetic energy as a gamma-ray $\gamma$ photon, for example when the daughter nucleus de-excites or when the positron later annihilates with an electron.
